title: Telnet Option Specifications
summary: Specifies the general form for Telnet options and how they are described. It replaces RFC 651 and is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Telnet can be extended with extra features. This memo is the recipe for writing down a new one.

questions: how are telnet option codes assigned
subtitle: How Telnet options get their codes and how each option has to be documented.

tldr.problem: Telnet options let hosts handle dissimilar devices better than the basic Network Virtual Terminal allows, but a single option code must never be used for several different options and options need to be well documented.
tldr.mechanism: One named individual assigns option codes, and each option is documented in five standard sections. The memo also explains subnegotiation, where parties agree with WILL and DO to discuss parameters and then exchange them with SB and SE.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard. Documentation is generally required before a code is assigned, though it may be waived for some experiments.

today: RFC 855 is an Internet Standard and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose of Telnet Options
sections.content:
Options let hosts find more elegant solutions to communication between dissimilar devices than the framework of the Network Virtual Terminal (NVT) allows. Hosts should be able to invent, test or discard options at will, but options that prove useful are expected to be supported by many hosts, so they should be carefully documented and publicized.

The memo specifies a method of option code assignment and standards for documentation. The assigner may waive complete documentation for some cases of experimentation, but in general documentation is required before a code is assigned. Options are publicized by publishing their documentation as RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: People can invent new tricks for Telnet. To keep things tidy, each trick gets a unique number and a written description.

sections.title: Documentation Sections
sections.content:
Option documentation should contain at least five sections:

  • Command Name and Option Code
  • Command Meanings: what each relevant Telnet command means for this option.
  • Default Specification: the assumptions for hosts that do not implement or use the option.
  • Motivation: why the option, or its particular form, was invented.
  • Description: text, a sample implementation or hints, enough that two implementations can communicate.

Option codes are assigned by Jonathan B. Postel at USC-ISI, as named in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: Every new trick needs a name tag, a list of what each signal means, what happens if you do not use it, why it exists, and enough detail to build it.

sections.title: Subnegotiation
sections.content:
Some options need more than a single option code, for example when a parameter must be passed. The approach has two steps. First, both parties agree to discuss the parameters: one proposes with DO or WILL followed by the option code, and the other accepts by returning WILL or DO. Second, the discussion happens with IAC SB ABC <parameters> IAC SE, where ABC stands for the option.

A receiver can find the end of the parameters by searching for IAC SE, even if it cannot parse them. Either party may stop at any time by sending WON'T or DON'T.
sections.plainLanguage: First both sides say "yes, let us talk about the details." Then they actually swap the details. Either one can stop the talk whenever they like.

sections.title: Avoiding Loops and Byte 255
sections.content:
Designers of options that need subnegotiation must take great care to avoid unending loops. For example, if each party accepts any parameter value and both suggest different values, the two may oscillate forever, each thinking it is only acknowledging the other's new proposal.

If parameters include a byte with the value 255, that byte must be doubled, following the general Telnet rules.
sections.plainLanguage: If two people each say "no, you pick" forever, nothing gets decided. Option designers must make sure the talk ends.
